title: Demonstrate an understanding of the feedlot environment

lessons.title: What a feedlot is and how it works
lessons.html:
The feedlot in the beef chain

Most beef in South Africa comes from feedlots. Weaner calves, usually around six to eight months old, are bought from cattle farmers, auctions and communal farmers, and are fed a high-energy ration in pens for a few months until they reach slaughter weight and the right fat cover. Large feedlots can hold tens of thousands of cattle, while smaller ones may finish a few hundred.

The flow of cattle

  1. Arrival – cattle are offloaded, weighed, given water and hay, and rested.
  2. Processing – each animal is tagged, weighed, vaccinated, dewormed and treated for external parasites according to the feedlot's health program.
  3. Adaptation – cattle start on a starter ration with more roughage and are stepped up gradually.
  4. Growing and finishing – rations with more grain give fast growth and fat cover.
  5. Marketing – cattle are selected, weighed and sent to the abattoir, often next to the feedlot.

Main areas of a feedlot

  • Receiving pens and processing area with crush, scale and handling facilities.
  • Production pens with feed bunkers and water troughs.
  • Hospital pens for sick cattle.
  • Feed mill or mixing area, commodity stores, silage bunkers.
  • Roads, drainage, manure storage and runoff dams.
  • Offices, workshop and staff facilities.

Every worker should know the layout, the pen numbering and the emergency points such as fire equipment and first aid boxes.

lessons.title: Daily routines and roles
lessons.html:
Who does what

A feedlot runs like a factory: the same tasks happen every day at fixed times, and each team depends on the others.

TeamMain work
Bunk readersScore bunkers and set the feed for each pen
Feed mill and feedersReceive ingredients, mix rations, deliver to bunkers
Pen riders and animal healthCheck pens for sick cattle, pull and treat them, keep treatment records
Processing and handlingReceive, process, move and load cattle
MaintenanceWater, fences, gates, machines, pen cleaning

Pen riding

Pen riders walk or ride through every pen daily, looking for cattle that are sick or injured. Signs include dull eyes, drooping ears, a nasal discharge, coughing, fast breathing, a swollen left side (bloat), lameness, loose dung and an animal standing apart. Respiratory disease is the most common problem in newly arrived cattle. Sick cattle are pulled quietly to the hospital pen and treated according to the vet's protocol, and treatments and withdrawal periods are recorded.

Low-stress handling

Cattle that are handled calmly eat sooner, get sick less and bruise less. Move slowly, use the animal's flight zone and point of balance, use flags or paddles instead of sticks, and never use electric prodders on the face or sensitive areas. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 forbids ill-treatment of animals.

Communication

Report problems at once: a pen without water, a broken gate, a sick animal, an unusual number of cattle off feed. Small problems become big losses quickly in a feedlot.

lessons.title: Health, safety and the environment
lessons.html:
Working safely

Feedlots are busy workplaces covered by the OHS Act 85 of 1993. The main hazards are large animals, moving vehicles and machinery, dust, chemicals and medicines.

  • Never stand in a crush or race with cattle; work from outside.
  • Always have an escape route when in a pen, and never enter a pen with an aggressive animal alone.
  • Stay visible to loaders, trucks and feed wagons; wear reflective clothing if issued.
  • Keep all guards on machines and never reach into mixers or augers while running.
  • Use gloves and protective equipment with medicines and dips; needle-stick injuries must be reported.
  • Wear a dust mask in dusty conditions and in the feed mill.

Bio-security

Many cattle from many sources mix in a feedlot, so disease control is critical. Follow the visitor rules, footbaths and vehicle routes. Keep hospital pens separate. Dispose of dead animals quickly by the approved method. Suspected notifiable diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease must be reported to the state veterinarian under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Environment

Feedlots produce large amounts of manure, runoff and odour. Pens are cleaned regularly; manure may be composted or sold as fertiliser. Rainwater running off pens must be held in runoff dams so it does not pollute rivers and groundwater, in line with the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Workers help by reporting overflowing dams, blocked drains and leaking troughs, and by not dumping waste.

Key points

  • A feedlot buys weaners, adapts them, and feeds them to slaughter weight.
  • Every team depends on the others; follow daily routines and times.
  • Pen riders look for sick cattle daily and pull them quietly to hospital pens.
  • Handle cattle calmly and work safely around animals and machines.
  • Control disease and protect water from feedlot runoff.
